source.title: Open problems in theory of nuclear open quantum systems

accepted.question_text: In continuum shell-model descriptions of nuclei as open quantum systems, a nucleus is coupled to scattering and decay channels through an energy-dependent effective Hamiltonian, and particle-emission thresholds appear as branch points of the scattering matrix. Is the formation of cluster states near decay thresholds, such as α-cluster states near α-emission thresholds or correlated two-neutron halo states near two-neutron emission thresholds, directly controlled by the branch point singularity of the relevant reaction channel, and what mechanism connects the threshold singularity to the channel-aligned cluster structure?
accepted.context_brief: Threshold branch points and cluster states

evidence.quote: Is there a connection between the branch point singularity at the particle emission threshold and the appearance of cluster states which reveal the structure of a corresponding reaction channel?

In particular, the entanglement of ISM wave functions due to their coupling to a common particle emission channel should be responsible for the omnipresence of clustering phenomena in states close to their cluster decay thresholds.
Cluster states close to decay thresholds. Left: Excited 0+ state in 12C (Hoyle state) just above the 8Be+α threshold. Right: Subthreshold halo ground state of 11Li.

accepted.question_text: In nuclear open quantum systems, how can one identify and predict which bound or unbound interacting-shell-model eigenstates are most strongly reorganized by coupling to scattering-continuum reaction channels, rather than assuming that continuum coupling produces a uniform instability of all states near a particle-emission threshold?
accepted.context_brief: States most affected by continuum coupling

evidence.quote: Which nuclear states are most impacted by the coupling to the scattering continuum?
As shown above, |Ecorr| is both state- and system-dependent, i.e., the continuum coupling does not induce a global instability of all ISM eigenstates close to the particle emission threshold.
On the contrary, for those ISM wave functions which are susceptible to the continuum coupling, the near-threshold instability is seen predominantly in a single pair of unperturbed ISM states.

accepted.question_text: For many-body nuclear systems whose energies lie in a narrow window around a reaction threshold, which structural properties are universal consequences of threshold physics, and which properties depend on the chosen nuclear Hamiltonian, effective interaction, or model realization?

evidence.quote: What can be said about properties of many-body systems in the narrow range of energies around the reaction threshold? Are those properties independent of any particular realization of the Hamiltonian?
The threshold features are generic: they are neither accidental nor arise from particular properties of the nuclear Hamiltonian.

On the contrary, the precise position of any exceptional point in the spectrum of eigenvalues of the energy-dependent effective Hamiltonian depends on the choice of the ISM Hamiltonian HQQ, the strength of the coupling term W(E), and the energy E of the system.

accepted.question_text: When neighboring nuclei with different proton and neutron numbers are interconnected through continuum reaction channels, what determines the size and internal organization of the resulting correlated domains, or clusters, of quantum states, and how do those features depend on the binding energies of the participating states?

evidence.quote: Many-body states in neighboring nuclear systems with different proton and neutron numbers become interconnected via continuum, forming correlated domains (clusters) of quantum states.
At present, little is known about the basic features of such clusters, e.g. a typical 'cluster size' and its dependence on binding properties of participating states.

When moving towards the particle drip lines, nuclei with different proton and neutron numbers become interconnected via continuum space, i.e., reaction channels, forming correlated domains of quantum states.

accepted.question_text: For neutron-rich isotopic chains such as oxygen and fluorine, how can one distinguish a shift in the neutron drip line caused by continuum-coupling-induced effective many-body interactions from an explanation based on explicitly introduced effective three-body interactions?

evidence.quote: Moreover, the continuum-coupling term generates effective many-body interactions in the internal space, even if it is originally two-body in the full space.
It has been found that the induced many-body interactions explain a significant shift in the neutron drip line for fluorine isotopes as compared to the oxygens.
Another explanation, explicitly invoking effective three-body interaction, has recently been suggested in Ref. [41]. These two scenarios could be difficult to distinguish.

accepted.question_text: How can the organization of interacting-shell-model eigenfunctions near a particle-emission threshold be made quantitatively predictive, especially for the ground state of 11Li where low-lying two-neutron and one-neutron emission thresholds are separated by less than 30 keV and may determine the relative weights of configurations associated with the two-neutron continuum of 9Li and with unbound 10Li channels?

evidence.quote: We are still far away from a quantitative understanding of the organization of ISM eigenfunctions near the particle emission threshold.

The structure of the ground state wave function of 11Li is a particularly interesting case-study due to an intricate sequence of low-lying two- and one-neutron emission thresholds which are separated by less than 30 keV (!).
This approximate degeneracy of two different emission thresholds may have important consequences on the structure of halo two-neutron pair.

The relative weights of configurations, such as [9Li(3/2−)]⊗[n2(0+)], corresponding to the two-neutron continuum of 9Li, and {[9Li(1/2−)]⊗[n(1/2−)]}1+⊗[n(1/2−)], {[9Li(1/2−)]⊗[n(1/2+)]}1−⊗[n(1/2+)], or {[9Li(3/2−)]⊗[n(1/2−)]}2+⊗[n(1/2−)], associated with an unbound 10Li, reflects the influence of these two almost degenerate branch points on the structure of the ground state wave function of 11Li.

accepted.question_text: How can low-energy exceptional points in nuclear open quantum systems, understood as double poles of the scattering matrix that arise from the interplay of Hermitian and non-Hermitian continuum coupling above threshold, be located or tested experimentally through reaction studies, for example through characteristic structures in elastic scattering phase shifts?

evidence.quote: The exceptional points, whose dramatic effects on the phase rigidity can be seen in Fig. 3, are also generic in Hamiltonian systems.
Hence, its finding provides the test of both the effective interaction and the configuration mixing in any OQS.
It has been found recently that low-energy exceptional points appear for realistic values of coupling to the continuum and hence could be accessible experimentally.
At low excitation energies, they could be seen, for example, as individual peaks associated with a jump by 2π of the elastic scattering phase shift.

Also in the neighborhood of an exceptional point for avoided crossing of resonances, this characteristic imprint of the scattering phase shift remains, which gives a real chance that traces of the exceptional could actually be searched for in reaction studies.

accepted.question_text: What sequence of theoretical developments is needed to build a unified theory of nuclear structure and nuclear reactions that treats bound states, resonances, and scattering states symmetrically, rather than keeping the discrete shell-model spectrum and scattering continuum artificially separated?

evidence.quote: What should be the most important steps in developing the theory that will truly unify nuclear structure and nuclear reactions?
Hence, the knowledge of nuclear structure depends on nuclear reactions and vice versa, and this cries out for a unified theoretical framework.

To understand the formation of a network of correlated states, e.g., the chain of isotopes from a well-bound 9Li to an unbound 12Li, a structure of the Hoyle resonance, and the radiative capture reactions, such 12C(α,γ)16O, a theoretical framework is required that would provide a unified approach to nuclear structure and reactions.
Such a theoretical framework could be developed based on the GSM.

accepted.question_text: How can the Gamow Shell Model be supplied with effective interactions that are accurate and systematic enough to study long isotopic or isotonic chains continuously from the valley of stability to the particle drip lines?

evidence.quote: Significant progress has also been made in applications of realistic interactions in GSM.

Still, much work is needed to develop appropriate effective interactions which would allow a systematic study of the structure of nuclear states in long isotopic or isotonic chains: from the valley of stability towards particle drip lines.

accepted.question_text: How can the Gamow Shell Model, which has mostly been applied to nuclear-structure calculations, be fully extended to reaction problems using a coupled-channel scattering formulation while preserving its treatment of bound states, resonances, and many-body scattering continua?

evidence.quote: This model, formulated in the Rigged Hilbert Space and using a complete Berggren ensemble, is a generalization of the nuclear ISM for a description of bound states, resonances, and many-body scattering continuum.
So far, most applications of the GSM have addressed nuclear structure phenomena.
Further progress can only be achieved if the method could be fully extended to reaction problems.
This can be achieved by the coupled-channel formulation of the scattering problem.

accepted.question_text: How can the dimensional growth of Gamow Shell Model calculations be controlled when increasing the number of active particles, given that each single-particle continuum state in the Berggren ensemble becomes a new shell in the many-body formulation?

evidence.quote: The 'dimensional catastrophe' in GSM when increasing the number of active particles is much more serious than in the standard ISM because each single-particle continuum state in the Berggren ensemble becomes a new shell in the many-body GSM formulation.
This acute problem has been alleviated by recent progress in the generalization of the Density Matrix Renormalization Group method to non-Hermitian, complex-symmetric matrix problems.

accepted.question_text: How can fast and scalable algorithms be developed for calculating the overlaps O_{c;n} between reaction channels and Gamow Shell Model many-body states, including the required coordinate transformations for heavier projectiles and for reactions with two-body asymptotic conditions?

evidence.quote: In the above equation, Hnm≡⟨Ψn|H|Ψm⟩ is the GSM Hamiltonian matrix and Oc;n≡⟨c;r|Ψn⟩ are overlaps of the reaction channel and the GSM many-body state.
Formally, Eq. (8) takes the same form independently of the choice of reaction channels; the whole complication is hidden in the overlaps Oc;n.
Their calculation is a formidable task for the GSM approach.
It requires a complicated change of the coordinate system which makes the calculation difficult for heavier projectiles, even for reactions with two-body asymptotic conditions.
Any future progress in the application of GSM to nuclear reactions is ultimately related to the progress in the development of new algorithms for fast calculation of overlaps.
